title: Detecting failure: timeouts, heartbeats and gray failure
goal: By the end, you can pick a timeout from measured delays and say what each choice costs, explain how TCP, the phi accrual detector and SWIM adapt to what they see, and spot a gray failure, where every health check says fine while customers see errors.
opening:
Your friend is hiking alone and promised to text "all good" every half hour. An hour passes with nothing. She may have fallen, or be in a valley with no signal, or her phone may be flat. From your sofa, they all look the same.

So you set a deadline for calling rescue. Too soon, and a helicopter finds her eating a sandwich. Too late, and help arrives late. It's tempting to keep one deadline, say an hour, for every walk. But she's never late in the city and often late in the mountains.

Partial failure: networks that lose, delay and duplicate left us right here. Silence has six causes and no timeout tells slow from dead, yet every system has to pick one.

In this lesson, we'll pick a timeout from measurements, then build one that learns what normal looks like. We'll see a thousand machines check with each other before they accuse one, and meet a machine that passes every check while failing its customers. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A group of machines treats one of them as dead if it hears no "I'm alive" message from it for 2 seconds. The machine sends one every second, and last week the slowest one took 1.4 seconds to arrive. Once a day, the machine's program stops completely for 3 seconds to clean up its memory. What happens once a day?
options: Nothing: 2 seconds is longer than the slowest message ever seen
The group declares the machine dead during the stop and hands its work to another, while it's alive and about to carry on
The machine keeps sending its "I'm alive" messages during the stop, so nobody notices
The machine notices its own stop and tells the group it was only slow
warmup.why: A stop of the whole program, here to clean up memory, stops every part of it, including the part that sends the "I'm alive" messages. So for 3 seconds the machine sends exactly what a dead machine sends: nothing. After 2 seconds the group can't tell the difference, and it acts. The machine can't warn anyone either, because nothing in it runs during the stop. The first option is the trap: last week's slowest message measured the network, not the machine's own stops.

sections.h: How long to wait: a timeout trades slow detection for false alarms
sections.body:
Let's put the hiker's problem into the payments app. Say one machine records every café's payments, and a second machine watches it, ready to hand its work to a spare machine, the standby, if it dies. The watcher can't see inside the first machine. All it can see is messages, so the first machine sends a small "I'm alive" message every second. That message is a **heartbeat**, like your friend's text. A healthy machine is never quiet for long, so silence becomes something the watcher can measure.

A program that decides when to suspect another machine is called a failure detector. Nearly every one in use works the same way: if nothing has arrived for T milliseconds, suspect the machine. T is a timeout, the same idea as the shop's 2-second wait in the last lesson. The only design question is T, and neither side of it is free.

Make T long, and a dead machine goes unnoticed for T. Payments sent to it pile up while nobody acts. At 2,000 payments a second, a 10-second timeout strands 20,000 of them, and then the standby still has to take over, a step called failover.

Make T short, and you raise false alarms: you declare a live machine dead because one heartbeat was slow. That costs more than it seems. The "dead" machine's work goes to the standby while the first one may still be doing it. That's the last lesson's double charge, with a whole machine's worth of work. In a bigger group, the load moves to machines that may already be busy. Their heartbeats slow down, and the next false alarm follows. A group of machines can talk itself into declaring everyone dead.

Bailis and Kingsbury's survey, from the last lesson, has a real case. Elasticsearch, a search program that runs on a cluster (a group of machines working as one), split into two clusters on about 1 start in 10. Its machines sometimes took longer than its 3-second timeout to find each other. Raising the timeout to 15 seconds fixed it.

**A timeout detects silence, not death.**

So you pick T from data. Measure the gaps between heartbeats, over days and over many machines, and put T beyond the gaps you see when things are normal. The figure shows the shape you'll find. Most gaps sit close to the 1-second interval, and a tail of longer gaps runs off to the right. Every gap past T is a false alarm, and every millisecond of T is time a dead machine goes unnoticed.

The lab has two links that make this concrete. One is a calm local network inside one building, a LAN, where each heartbeat takes 1 to 5 ms. The other is a jittery long-distance link between two regions, groups of cloud datacenters far apart, called a WAN. There each heartbeat takes 30 to 830 ms. (Jitter is how much the delay varies.) On the calm link the gaps stay within a few milliseconds of 1 second, and a 1.5-second timeout notices a crash in 1.5 seconds with no false alarms in 5 minutes. On the jittery link, the same timeout fires 15 times in 5 minutes, on a machine that never failed. A 3-second timeout is quiet on both, and makes the calm link wait twice as long as it needs to.

One number can't suit both links. Next, we'll stop using one number.

try.title: Fixed timeouts on two links
steps: Predict: a 1.5-second timeout on the jittery link, where each heartbeat takes 30 to 830 ms. How many false alarms in 5 minutes?

Run the demo. It sends a heartbeat every second for 300 s, kills the machine, and asks each detector every 10 ms whether it suspects the machine. (The output calls the machine a node, the usual word for one machine in a group.) Ignore the rows that start with `phi` until the next section.
Why does the 3-second timeout take 3,009 ms to notice the crash on the calm link, but 3,719 ms on the jittery one?
try.expect:
```text
The node dies at 300 s

calm LAN: each heartbeat takes 1 to 5 ms
detector          false alarms  suspected while alive   detection
fixed 1,500 ms               0                   0 ms     1509 ms
fixed 3,000 ms               0                   0 ms     3009 ms
fixed 6,000 ms               0                   0 ms     6009 ms
phi > 8                      0                   0 ms     1569 ms
phi > 12                     0                   0 ms     1709 ms

jittery WAN: each heartbeat takes 30 to 830 ms
detector          false alarms  suspected while alive   detection
fixed 1,500 ms              15                1540 ms     2219 ms
fixed 3,000 ms               0                   0 ms     3719 ms
fixed 6,000 ms               0                   0 ms     6719 ms
phi > 8                      0                   0 ms     3449 ms
phi > 12                     0                   0 ms     3889 ms
```

On the jittery link, a gap is 1,000 ms plus the difference between two delays, so it can reach 1,800 ms, and 15 gaps in 300 crossed 1.5 seconds. `suspected while alive` adds up the time a detector spent suspecting a machine that was fine. Detection is measured from the crash. The machine sends its last heartbeat just before it dies, but the timeout starts when that heartbeat arrives, so on the jittery link the last heartbeat's own delay (about 700 ms here) is added.

sections.h: A timeout that learns what normal looks like
sections.body:
TCP, the rules most programs use to send data over a network, met this problem decades ago. When it sends data, it has to decide how long to wait for the ACK, the receiver's "got it", before it resends. That wait is its retransmission timeout, and it isn't a fixed number. RFC 6298, the document that sets the rule, keeps two running numbers. One is a smoothed round-trip time, a running average of how long the ACKs take. The other is a smoothed variation, how far each round trip usually lands from that average. The timeout is the average plus four times the variation. Each new measurement moves the average by 1/8 of the difference, and the variation by 1/4. A steady path gets a tight timeout and a jumpy path a loose one, and nobody chooses either. (Linux adds a floor of 200 ms.)

You do the same for your hiking friend without thinking. On the city walk she's never late, so 35 minutes of silence would worry you. On the mountain route she's often 40 minutes late, so you'd give her much longer.

The **phi accrual detector** (Naohiro Hayashibara and colleagues, 2004) brings this idea to heartbeats. It doesn't answer yes or no. It reports a level of suspicion, phi, that grows the longer the silence lasts. Phi comes from a question: if the machine were healthy, how likely would it be to stay quiet this long? Phi writes that chance as a count of zeros. Phi 1 means one chance in 10, phi 2 one in 100, and phi 8 one in 100 million. (In maths terms, phi is minus the base-10 logarithm of the chance.) The detector suspects the machine once phi passes a threshold, often 8.

To work out the chance, the detector needs a picture of the usual gaps. Cassandra, a database that runs on many machines, uses a simple one that needs only the average gap. (The Partitioning track's lesson Inside a Cassandra cluster: the token ring, gossip and failure detection showed it running.) The original paper uses a bell curve instead, and so does Akka, a toolkit for programs that run on many machines. A bell curve is the hump-shaped curve that people's heights or exam marks usually follow. Both take the average and the standard deviation of the last 1,000 gaps. The standard deviation measures how far the gaps usually are from the average, and it's what lets the detector adapt to jitter. The lab builds this version.

Let's work through the numbers. On a bell curve, phi passes 8 when the silence is about 5.6 standard deviations longer than the average gap. On the calm link the gaps barely vary, so the detector's floor of 100 ms on the standard deviation applies. It suspects after about 1,000 + 5.6 × 100 = 1,561 ms of silence. On the jittery link the standard deviation is about 330 ms, so it waits about 2,800 ms. Each link gets its own timeout from its own history. Phi 8 raises no false alarms on either link, and it notices a crash in about 1.6 seconds on the calm one and 3.4 on the jittery one.

Now freeze the machine for 4 seconds, as a long pause for garbage collection would. (That's when a Java or Kotlin program stops everything to clear out memory it no longer uses.) Every detector that notices crashes in under 4 seconds suspects the paused machine: phi on both links, the 3-second timeout, all of them. That isn't bad tuning. For those 4 seconds a paused machine and a dead one send exactly the same thing, nothing. The only way never to suspect a 4-second pause is never to suspect anything sooner than 4 seconds.

There is a second effect. The 4-second gap now sits among the 1,000 gaps the detector remembers, and it raises the standard deviation. So phi takes about 2 seconds instead of 1.6 to notice the next real crash. Cassandra doesn't record gaps longer than 2 seconds, for exactly that reason.

Here the hiking picture breaks. A friend who turns up after you called rescue is glad to be found. A machine that wakes from a pause carries on with what it was doing, perhaps still sure it's the one in charge. Lesson 4 is about those pauses.

**A detector only suspects. Make a wrong guess cost time, never data.**

The rest of this track keeps that promise, with fencing tokens in lesson 5 and majorities in lesson 7. The detector's job is to make the common case fast. Watching one machine is the easy case, though. Next, we'll watch a thousand.

try.title: A 4-second pause
steps: Run the demo with `pause`. The machine freezes for 4 seconds at 199 s, then runs normally until it dies at 300 s.
Which detectors raise exactly one false alarm? Which raise none, and what does that cost them at 300 s?
Compare phi's detection time on the calm link with the run without a pause. Where do the extra 430 ms come from?

```text
The node freezes for 4 s at 199 s, then dies at 300 s

calm LAN: each heartbeat takes 1 to 5 ms
detector          false alarms  suspected while alive   detection
fixed 1,500 ms               1                2500 ms     1509 ms
fixed 3,000 ms               1                1000 ms     3009 ms
fixed 6,000 ms               0                   0 ms     6009 ms
phi > 8                      1                2440 ms     1999 ms
phi > 12                     1                2300 ms     2239 ms

jittery WAN: each heartbeat takes 30 to 830 ms
detector          false alarms  suspected while alive   detection
fixed 1,500 ms              16                4070 ms     2109 ms
fixed 3,000 ms               1                1030 ms     3609 ms
fixed 6,000 ms               0                   0 ms     6609 ms
phi > 8                      1                1380 ms     3619 ms
phi > 12                     1                 960 ms     4129 ms
```

Every detector faster than 4 seconds raised one false alarm for the pause (the 1.5-second timeout on the jittery link has its 15 jitter alarms on top). Only the 6-second timeout stayed quiet, and it pays 6 seconds for every real crash. Phi on the calm link now needs 1,999 ms instead of 1,569 ms. The 4,001 ms gap is one of the 1,000 in its window and roughly doubles the standard deviation it works out, so the detector stays more patient until that gap leaves the window.

sections.h: Watching a thousand machines: SWIM asks others before it accuses
sections.body:
One watcher with heartbeats works for a handful of machines. In a big group, every machine has to keep an eye on the others. If every machine sends heartbeats to every other, that's n × (n − 1) messages a second for n machines. With 1,000 machines, it's about a million messages a second to learn that nearly everyone is fine. And each verdict rests on one path. If the link from A to B is the broken one, A suspects B while everyone else can reach it.

SWIM (Abhinandan Das, Indranil Gupta and Ashish Motivala, 2002) fixes both, and the stepper below walks through one round. The Partitioning track's Cassandra lesson sketched it too. The machines in the group are called members. Once every protocol period, a fixed slot of time, each member sends a ping, a tiny "are you there?" message also called a probe, to one member chosen at random. The target answers with an ack, a short "yes". If no ack comes back in time, the member doesn't accuse yet. It asks k other members to ping the target for it, with a message called a ping-req. Only if none of them gets an ack does it mark the target **suspect**.

A suspect isn't dead. The news spreads by gossip, the way a rumour spreads through a school. Each member passes it on, riding along on the pings and acks it sends anyway, so spreading it costs no extra messages. When the suspect hears the rumour about itself, it answers by raising its incarnation number, a counter that only that member may increase. A higher number beats any rumour about a lower one. If no answer comes before the suspicion timeout ends, the member is declared dead.

The cost per member doesn't grow with the group. Each member sends about the same number of messages a second, whether there are 10 members or 10,000. The expected time until someone notices a crash stays the same too. HashiCorp, a company that makes tools for running programs on many machines, uses SWIM in its library memberlist. On a local network, memberlist sends a probe every second, waits 500 ms for the ack, and asks 3 others for an indirect check.

Lifeguard (Armon Dadgar, James Phillips and Jon Currey at HashiCorp, 2017) looked at the false alarms that SWIM still raised. Many came from the accuser, not the accused. A member that is starved of processor time, or paused, misses acks that did arrive, and then suspects healthy members. It's the friend on the sofa whose own phone has no signal. So in Lifeguard each member keeps a health score about itself. The score gets worse when its own probes fail, or when it has to deny rumours about itself. While the score is bad, the member probes less often and waits longer for acks, up to 8 times longer in memberlist. A suspicion's timeout also starts long, and shrinks as more members confirm it on their own. HashiCorp reported more than 50 times fewer false alarms when processors were overloaded, with no slower detection of real failures.

**Before you accuse another machine, check yourself.**

Cassandra's version of this is blunter: a machine that was itself frozen for more than 5 seconds marks nobody down when it wakes. If you write a watcher of your own, give it the same guard. Check how late the watcher's own loop ran, using `System.nanoTime()`, a clock that only counts forward (the next lesson explains it). Compare that with when the loop should have run, and skip that round's verdicts if the watcher was the one not listening.

So far, every detector has asked one question: does the machine answer? Next, we'll meet a machine that answers every check and still fails its customers.

stepper.intro: Five members of a group that runs memberlist with its local-network settings: a probe every second, 500 ms to wait for an ack, and k = 3 indirect checks.

frames.say: C, D and E each ping B, each along its own path. If any of them gets an ack, it passes it back to A, and the round ends with B alive. The path from A was the problem, and nobody suspected anyone.

Now A has more than its own view.</text></svg>
frames.say: This time none of them hears back either. Four paths have failed, not one, so the evidence is much stronger than A's own timeout. It's still not proof: B may be paused.

frames.say: A marks B **suspect**, not dead. The news travels by gossip: it piggybacks, or rides along, on the pings and acks that members send anyway, so spreading it costs no extra messages. A suspicion timeout starts.

The suspicion is dropped.</text></svg>
frames.say: B was only paused. When it hears the rumour about itself, it raises its incarnation to 5 and gossips *alive, incarnation 5*. A higher incarnation beats any suspicion about a lower one, so every member drops it.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 316" role="img" aria-label="If B is really dead, the suspicion times out"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><rect class="box" x="20" y="112" width="130" height="50" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="85.0" y="133.0" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="85.0" y="151.0" text-anchor="middle">member</text><rect class="box-bad" x="490" y="112" width="130" height="50" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="555.0" y="133.0" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="555.0" y="151.0" text-anchor="middle">dead</text><rect class="box" x="170" y="20" width="130" height="50" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="235.0" y="41.0" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="235.0" y="59.0" text-anchor="middle">member</text><rect class="box" x="340" y="20" width="130" height="50" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="405.0" y="41.0" text-anchor="middle">D</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="405.0" y="59.0" text-anchor="middle">member</text><rect class="box" x="255" y="210" width="130" height="50" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="320.0" y="231.0" text-anchor="middle">E</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="320.0" y="249.0" text-anchor="middle">member</text><rect class="box-bad" x="20" y="272" width="600" height="34" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="320" y="294" text-anchor="middle">If no refutation arrives within the suspicion timeout, B is declared dead.</text></svg>
frames.say: If B really crashed, nobody answers the rumour. When the suspicion timeout ends (in memberlist it grows slowly with the size of the group), B is declared **dead**, and that news spreads the same way. Lifeguard makes this timeout start long and shrink as other members confirm the suspicion.

sections.h: Gray failure: every check says fine while customers see errors
sections.body:
Every detector so far asks one question: does the machine answer? Peng Huang and colleagues, most of them at Microsoft (HotOS 2017, a research workshop), found that most of the incidents they studied in Azure, Microsoft's cloud, weren't crashes. They were **gray failures**: a part that keeps passing its health checks while it fails at its real job. A health check is a small test a watcher runs against a program now and then, such as asking "are you up?".

Their key idea is differential observability: different parts of the system see different things. The part that suffers, such as the program or the user, sees the failure. The part that decides whether to act doesn't: the failure detector, or the load balancer that spreads requests over copies of a program. In one of their cases, a driver bug broke the network inside some virtual machines, pretend computers that share a real one. (A driver is the small program that runs one piece of hardware.) The virtual machines kept looking healthy, because their heartbeats went out through a helper on the real machine, over a local channel that didn't use the broken network. Nothing fixed them until users complained.

Having many spare parts makes this worse, in a way you can work out. A datacenter, a building full of machines, has a network of switches, boxes that pass packets (small parcels of data) along. In the middle sit many equal core switches that join all the others, and each packet crosses one of them. When a core switch dies, the network sends traffic around it. When one drops some packets and still answers its own checks, nothing goes around it. Now take a request that fans out to m machines: it's split into m smaller requests, and each one takes a random path. With n core switches, the chance that the request touches the gray one is 1 − ((n − 1)/n)^m. For one small request, with 16 switches, that's 6%. For a request with a fan-out of 100, it's 99.8%. A fanned-out request is as slow as its slowest part, so one gray switch slows nearly every large request. And more switches means more chances that one of them is gray.

Health checks lie the same way inside one program. Big services run many copies of the same program, and the load balancer passes each request to one of them. Picture the payments program with 20 database connections that it opens once and reuses. A check that only proves the program answers stays green (healthy) while all 20 connections are stuck behind a lock, and every payment times out. (A lock lets one piece of work at a time use something. Here, something holds it and never lets go.) The Try shows that case. A deeper check borrows a connection and runs `SELECT 1`, a database question that does nothing except get answered. It catches the problem, but it has a cost of its own. When the shared database is slow, every copy of the program fails its deep check at the same moment. A load balancer that removes them all turns a slow database into a full outage, where nothing works. AWS, Amazon's cloud, describes the usual answer in its Builders' Library article on health checks. Its load balancers fail open: when every copy fails, they send traffic to all of them anyway.

Tools that run many copies of a program usually ask two separate questions. Is this copy alive? If not, restart it. Is it ready? If not, stop sending it requests, but leave it running. A deep check belongs to the second question only. Wire it to the first, and a slow database gets every copy restarted at once, and the fresh copies hit the slow database harder while they start. Kubernetes, a popular program that starts and watches other programs across many machines, calls these the liveness and readiness checks.

**Judge health by what customers see.**

The better fix closes the gap between what each part sees. A synthetic payment, a made-up test payment that the company sends through the whole path every few seconds, sees what a customer sees. So does outlier detection. A proxy, a program that sits between the shop and the copies, watches each copy's real answers. It stops sending to a copy whose requests keep failing, however green that copy's health check is. Envoy, a widely used proxy, does this.

Every detector in this lesson measured time: gaps, timeouts, how late a loop ran. Next, we'll find out how far a machine can trust its own clock.

try.title: Fan-out and a health check that lies
steps: Predict: with 64 core switches, what share of requests with a fan-out of 100 touch the one gray switch?

Run the demo. Part 1 prints `chanceToTouchGray` for 4, 16 and 64 switches. Part 2 runs a payments program whose 20 database connections are stuck from 20 s to 50 s. Two kinds of health check test it every second: a shallow one (alive) and a deep one (ready).
Which check would have taken the copy out of the load balancer? Which would have done the same to every copy if the database itself were slow?
try.expect:
```text
Chance that one request touches the one gray switch
switches    fan-out 1         10        100      1,000
4               25.0%      94.4%     100.0%     100.0%
16               6.3%      47.6%      99.8%     100.0%
64               1.6%      14.6%      79.3%     100.0%

A payments service, 100 requests a second; all 20 database connections stuck from 20 s to 50 s
seconds        users served   shallow check (live)   deep check (ready)
0-10                   100%                 10 of 10               10 of 10
10-20                  100%                 10 of 10               10 of 10
20-30                    0%                 10 of 10                0 of 10
30-40                    0%                 10 of 10                0 of 10
40-50                    0%                 10 of 10                0 of 10
50-60                  100%                 10 of 10               10 of 10
60-70                  100%                 10 of 10               10 of 10
```

With 64 switches and a fan-out of 100, 79% of requests cross the gray one, and at a fan-out of 1,000 all of them do. In part 2, the shallow check reports 10 of 10 in every 10-second window, while customers get nothing for 30 seconds: that's differential observability in one table. The deep check sees it, and for the same reason it would fail on every copy at once if the database itself were slow.

AWS Builders' Library: Implementing health checks

compare.title: A shallow check and a deep check

a.label: Shallow: is the program answering?
a.title: AliveCheck.kt

b.label: Deep: can it reach the database?
b.title: ReadyCheck.kt

compare.note: The left check can't see a gray failure in the database path: if the program can run this function, it says yes. The right one can, because it needs the same pooled connection a payment needs, and `isValid(1)` gives the database one second to answer. That's also its danger. If the database is slow for everyone, every copy turns not-ready together. Let the deep check stop traffic to a copy (ready), and never let it restart one (alive).

worked.title: Build a phi accrual detector from a fixed timeout

steps.say: Start with a fixed timeout: remember when the last heartbeat came, and suspect once the silence is longer than T. One number for every link.
Record what normal looks like: the gaps between heartbeats, in a window of the last 1,000. Running sums keep every check equally cheap, however big the window.
Turn the window into an average and a standard deviation, with a floor, so that a perfectly regular link doesn't suspect a gap 1 ms longer than usual.
steps.code:
val mean = sum / gaps.size
val variance = max(sumOfSquares / gaps.size - mean * mean, 0.0)
val stdDev = max(sqrt(variance), minStdDevMs)            // 100 ms by default

steps.say: Ask the bell curve how unusual this silence is, and take minus the log. `probabilityLater` is the share of a bell curve, with that average and spread, that lies beyond the silence: the chance that a healthy machine would stay quiet even longer.
steps.code:
val p = probabilityLater((nowMs - last).toDouble(), mean, stdDev)
return -log10(p)                                          // 1: one in 10; 8: one in 100 million

steps.say: Check the numbers by hand. The gaps are exactly 1,000 ms, so the 100 ms floor applies. At 1,000 ms of silence, p = 0.5 and phi = 0.30. At 1,500 ms the silence is 5 deviations late: p = 2.9 × 10⁻⁷ and phi = 6.54. Phi passes 8 at about 1,561 ms, 5.6 deviations late.

lab.title: Fixed timeouts against phi accrual, and the gray switch
steps: Read `Heartbeats.kt`, which is given. `arrivals` turns a `Scenario` (a link, pauses, a crash) into the times when heartbeats arrive, in virtual time, a pretend clock that the program moves forward itself. `score` asks a detector every 10 ms whether it suspects the machine, and counts false alarms and how long detection took. Run the tests from the `labs` folder: all 17 fail.

Exercise 1: `FixedTimeoutDetector`. Suspect only when the silence is strictly longer than the timeout, and never before the first heartbeat. Run `--tests 'sfz.dist.l02.ScenarioTest'`: the fixed-timeout tests pass, including the two jqwik properties about a 4-second pause. (jqwik is a test library that runs one check with many random inputs.)

Exercise 2: `PhiAccrualDetector.heartbeat` and `phi`. Keep the last `windowSize` gaps. Use the population standard deviation (divide by the number of gaps, not by one less), with `minStdDevMs` as its floor, and return 0.0 until there is a gap. `DetectorTest` checks phi against values worked out by hand: 0.30 at the average gap, and 6.54 at five standard deviations past it.
Exercise 3: `chanceToTouchGray`, one line. Then run all 17 tests and read `ScenarioTest`: it states this lesson's claims as numbers.
hints: `last?.let { nowMs - it > timeoutMs } ?: false` is the whole of `suspects`.
An `ArrayDeque<Long>` with `addLast` and `removeFirst` keeps the window. Working out the average and the variance by looping over 1,000 gaps on every check is fine here; running sums are faster.
Population variance is the average of the squares minus the square of the average. Floor it at 0.0 before `sqrt`, because rounding can make it a tiny negative number.
`(1.0 - 1.0 / paths).pow(fanOut)` is the chance that every smaller request misses the gray path.

drill.title: Phi by hand and in code
drill.prompt: From memory, write `phi(nowMs)` given `gaps`, `last` and `minStdDevMs`, calling `probabilityLater(elapsed, mean, stdDev)`. Then, without running anything: the gaps average 1,000 ms, with a standard deviation of 300 ms. Roughly when does phi pass 8, and why does a fixed 1.5-second timeout misbehave on the same link?

recap: A failure detector turns silence into suspicion with a timeout. A long timeout notices crashes late. A short one declares live machines dead, which repeats their work and moves their load until the whole group can tip over.

Pick the timeout from measured gaps, or let it adapt. TCP waits the average round trip plus four times its variation, and phi accrual turns the average and spread of recent heartbeat gaps into a level of suspicion.

SWIM checks before it accuses (a ping-req through k members, suspect before dead, an answer with a higher incarnation number) at a cost per member that doesn't grow with the group. Lifeguard makes a struggling accuser slow down.
Gray failure is differential observability: customers see the failure and the detector doesn't. With a fan-out of m over n paths, 1 − ((n − 1)/n)^m of requests touch one gray path.
Health checks lie unless they take the customer's path. Keep the alive check shallow, put the database in the ready check, and judge health by real or made-up payments.

The limit: while a machine is paused it looks exactly like a dead one, so any detector faster than your longest pause will suspect it. Correctness has to come from fencing and majorities, not from the detector.
closing:
We started with a friend on a hike and a deadline for calling rescue. Machines make the same choice every second: wait long and notice crashes late, or wait short and raise false alarms. The best detectors learn what normal looks like, ask others before they accuse, and check themselves first.

Look at the "online" or "last seen" marker next to a friend in a messaging app. It's a heartbeat detector. Notice how long it takes to change after they close the app, and ask whether a flat phone looks any different from one in flight mode.

Next, we'll look at the clocks every detector relies on, and find out why two machines can't agree on what time it is.

quiz.q: From Partial failure: networks that lose, delay and duplicate. The detector suspects the issuer's machine, so the shop sends `pay-77`, which it had already sent, to the issuer's standby machine instead. The first machine was only paused. What can happen to `pay-77`?
options: Nothing: the suspicion proves the first machine never handled it
It's charged twice, unless both machines check the same idempotency key in a store they share
It's lost, because a suspected machine throws away its waiting requests
The standby refuses it, because TCP spots the copy
quiz.why: A suspicion is not proof. The paused machine still holds `pay-77` in memory and charges it when it wakes, and the standby charges it too. The idempotency key from the last lesson stops the double charge only if both machines record keys in the same place, in the same transaction as the charge. TCP can't help: the second copy went over a different connection to a different machine.

quiz.q: A phi accrual detector has seen 1,000 gaps that average 1,000 ms, with a standard deviation of 20 ms. Its floor for the standard deviation is 100 ms. Roughly how long a silence makes phi pass 8?
options: About 1,110 ms
About 1,560 ms
About 8,000 ms
About 18,400 ms
quiz.why: The floor replaces the measured 20 ms with 100 ms, and phi 8 is about 5.6 standard deviations past the average: 1,000 + 5.6 × 100 ≈ 1,560 ms. Without the floor it would be about 1,110 ms, which would turn every small hiccup on a calm local network into a false alarm. 18,400 ms is what Cassandra's simpler model gives for a 1-second average, because it ignores the spread entirely.

quiz.q: In SWIM, member A gets no ack from B, and none of A's three ping-req helpers gets one either. B is alive but was paused for 3 seconds. What stops the group from declaring B dead?
options: B is only suspected at first; when it wakes and hears the rumour, it raises its incarnation number and gossips that it's alive, which beats the suspicion
A waits for a second protocol period before it suspects anyone
The helpers' acks arrive later and cancel the suspicion
Nothing: SWIM declares B dead as soon as the indirect pings fail
quiz.why: SWIM keeps suspect and dead apart. During the suspicion timeout, B can answer with a higher incarnation number, a counter only B may raise, and every member believes the higher number. Late acks to an old ping don't cancel anything, and SWIM doesn't wait another period before it suspects.

quiz.q: A search request is split into 200 smaller requests to 200 machines, over a network with 32 equal core switches. One switch drops 5% of packets but still answers its own checks. About what share of search requests touch it?
options: About 3%
About 5%
About 50%
About 100%
quiz.why: 1 − (31/32)^200 ≈ 0.998. Each smaller request has a 1-in-32 chance, but with 200 of them nearly every search has at least one on the gray switch, and a search is only as fast as its slowest part. 3% is the chance for one smaller request, and 5% is the switch's own loss rate.

quiz.q: A tool that runs the payments program restarts any copy whose alive check fails. The team makes the alive check run `SELECT 1` on the database, with a 2-second limit. One evening the database slows to 3-second answers. What happens?
options: Nothing: the alive check only matters when a copy starts
Only the copies with slow connections are restarted, which fixes them
Every copy fails the alive check at about the same time and is restarted, and the fresh copies add load to the slow database
The copies stop getting requests but keep running
quiz.why: A deep check measures a database that every copy shares, so every copy fails it together, and a failed alive check means a restart. Restarts can't make the database faster, and the fresh copies add load to it. The last option is what a failed ready check does, which is where a database check belongs. Even there, all copies leaving at once needs the fail-open rule from the AWS article.

flashcards.front: What does a short failure-detection timeout cost?
flashcards.back: False alarms: live machines declared dead, their work repeated, and their load moved onto other machines, which can spread.

flashcards.front: How does TCP set its retransmission timeout (RFC 6298)?
flashcards.back: The smoothed round-trip time plus four times its smoothed variation, moved by 1/8 and 1/4 of each new difference. Linux sets a floor of 200 ms.
A healthy machine would stay this quiet with a chance of one in 100 million, judged from recent heartbeat gaps. On a bell curve, that's about 5.6 standard deviations past the average gap.

flashcards.front: Why can no detector tell a 4-second pause from a crash in under 4 seconds?
flashcards.back: Both send nothing during that time. Only waiting longer than the pause tells them apart.

Ping a random member. If no ack comes, ask k others to ping it (a ping-req). If still nothing, mark it suspect and gossip that. It answers with a higher incarnation number, or is declared dead when the suspicion timeout ends.
The part that suffers from a failure (the program, the user) sees it, while the part that detects and reacts (health checks, the load balancer) doesn't. It's the mark of a gray failure.

flashcards.front: Alive check or ready check: which may ask the database?
flashcards.back: The ready check: failing it takes a copy out of rotation without restarting it. The alive check should catch only what a restart cures.

terms.plain: A small message a machine sends at a regular interval that says only "I'm alive", so silence can be measured.
A program that decides when to suspect that another machine has failed, usually from how long it has been silent.
A detector suspecting a machine that is alive, only slow or paused.
A detector that reports a level of suspicion from how unusual the current silence is, given recent heartbeat gaps.
A way for a big group to watch its members: random pings, indirect pings through k members, suspicion before death, and an answer by incarnation number.
A counter that only a member may raise about itself, used to beat older suspicions.
A part that passes its health checks while failing at its real work.
The failure is visible to the users of a part, but not to whatever watches it.

explain_back.prompt: A friend runs a payments database on three machines. One of them, the leader, takes all the changes. They want to cut the time before a silent leader is declared dead from 10 seconds to 1 second, "because failing over should be fast". Explain what that changes, and what you would measure first.
explain_back.answer: A timeout doesn't detect crashes, it detects silence. A leader is silent during a garbage-collection pause, a stall in its virtual machine or a slow patch of network, as well as after a crash. At 10 seconds, we pay up to 10 seconds of stalled changes for each real crash. At 1 second we'd notice crashes sooner, but we'd also declare the leader dead each time it pauses or a queue fills for a second. Each false failover is risky. A new leader is chosen while the old one may wake up and keep accepting changes until it's stopped, and the extra failovers move load at the worst moment. So first I'd measure the heartbeat gaps and the leader's own pauses over a few weeks, including the slowest ones, and put the timeout past the longest pause we're willing to treat as normal. Better still, use an adaptive detector like phi accrual, which waits longer on a jittery link and less on a calm one. Whatever we choose, correctness mustn't depend on it: the old leader has to be fenced off with a number that marks the current leader (lesson 5), so that a wrong suspicion costs time, not data.

deeper.body:
**Fail-slow hardware.** Gray failure has a hardware cousin. Haryadi Gunawi and colleagues' "Fail-Slow at Scale" (FAST 2018, a storage research conference) collected 101 reports, from 12 institutions, of disks, SSDs, processors, memory and network parts that kept working far below their normal speed. It also described the long chains of trouble they set off in clusters that only knew "up" and "down". TigerBeetle, a database built for financial records, lists a disk that becomes very slow without returning an error among the faults its tests inject.

**The accrual idea in other places.** Akka's cluster uses the bell-curve phi detector with a threshold of 8, and adds an *acceptable heartbeat pause* to the average: a budget for garbage-collection pauses it shouldn't suspect. Its documentation suggests a threshold of 12 in clouds with more jitter. Cassandra's simpler variant ignores the spread and depends only on the average gap, which is easier to work out and more patient on calm links.

**Detectors in theory.** Tushar Chandra and Sam Toueg (1996) sorted failure detectors by how wrong they may be, for example "eventually every crashed machine is suspected, and eventually some working machine is never suspected". They showed which kinds are enough to solve consensus, the problem of getting machines to agree on one value. Lesson 7 of this track and the Consistency and consensus track use that result: consensus methods stay safe with a detector that is often wrong, and only need it to be right eventually to make progress.

*Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2nd edition, chapter 9, discusses timeouts and machines that limp along, with more references.
